- Within panels, multiple **lines** compare categories (e.g., male vs female, or different substances/behaviors).

1. **Chart type**: Multi-panel line chart (small multiples of time-series line charts).

2. **Layout techniques**:  
- Uses **small multiples/faceting**: each panel shows a different outcome/measure.  
- Within panels, multiple **lines** compare categories (e.g., male vs female, or different substances/behaviors).  
- No stacking.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Percentage / share of teens | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Measure / outcome (e.g., ever tried vaping, recently drank alcohol, ever had sex, watch television at least 3 hours a day, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; text labels inside panels |
| Substance/behavior within panel (e.g., cigarettes, vaping, alcohol, marijuana, cocaine; sex vs unprotected sex; television vs sleep) | Categorical/nominal | Separate line color/hue; direct text labels |
| Sex (male, female) | Categorical/nominal | Separate line color/hue; direct text labels |

- Seriously considered suicide
- Made a suicide plan

raw_comment: The graphs show trends in health-related behaviors among US high school students from 1989 to 2019. The data is based on surveys of more than 10,000 high school students from public and private schools across the country, collected by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) as part of the Youth Risk Behavior Surveillance System (YRBSS), which monitors six categories of health-related behaviors. The story that the graphs tell is that there has been a significant shift in the health-related behaviors of US high school students over the past 30 years, with some positive changes, but also some concerning negative trends.

raw_comment: These graphs show the trends in health-related behaviors among high school students from 1989 to 2019. The graphs reveal changes in the prevalence and severity of behaviors related to physical activity, nutrition, substance use, and sexual activity over time. For instance, the data shows that from 1989 to 2019, high school students have been consuming fewer fruits and vegetables, drinking less milk, engaging in less physical activity, and having less sex, but they have also been using electronic cigarettes, marijuana, and prescription drugs more frequently. The graphs provide important insights into the health behaviors of American teenagers and can help identify areas where more intervention and prevention efforts may be needed.

image_description:
1. **Chart type**: Multi-panel line chart (small multiples of time-series line charts).

2. **Layout techniques**:  
- Uses **small multiples/faceting**: each panel shows a different outcome/measure.  
- Within panels, multiple **lines** compare categories (e.g., male vs female, or different substances/behaviors).  
- No stacking.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Percentage / share of teens | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Measure / outcome (e.g., ever tried vaping, recently drank alcohol, ever had sex, watch television at least 3 hours a day, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; text labels inside panels |
| Substance/behavior within panel (e.g., cigarettes, vaping, alcohol, marijuana, cocaine; sex vs unprotected sex; television vs sleep) | Categorical/nominal | Separate line color/hue; direct text labels |
| Sex (male, female) | Categorical/nominal | Separate line color/hue; direct text labels |

**Visible panel measures/outcomes**:
- Ever tried vaping
- Ever tried cigarettes
- Recently drank alcohol
- Ever used marijuana
- Ever used cocaine
- Ever had sex
- Last sex was unprotected
- Watch television at least 3 hours a day
- Get at least 8 hours of sleep
- Use a smartphone, tablet, computer or game console at least 3 hours a day, not including school work
- Persistently felt sad or hopeless
- Seriously considered suicide
- Made a suicide plan
- Attempted suicide
- Injured in a suicide attempt and needed medical treatment

raw_comment:
The upper set of graphs shows declines in risky behavior: vaping, smoking , using alcohol and cocaine, and having unprotected sex.  Use of marijuana is on the rise again (30%).
 I was surprised to notice the downward trend in sleeping and television watching, until I noted  the increase in electronic devices usage.  It may explain the decline in watching TV: everything is done on the phone, tablet, or other device, these days.
Trends in the upper set of graphs seems more positive; the lower set of graphs presents a different picture: between 2009 and 2019, teens feeling sadness and hopelessness are on the rise, as are the number of those who seriously considered suicide, those who made a suicide plan, and those who attempted suicide.
I wonder if there is a correlation between lack of traditional methods of “escape” (alcohol, tobacco) and the rise in feelings of negativity.  In other words, does it alleviate sadness if we imbibe nicotine and alcohol?  Or does the rise in marijuana use cause paranoid reactions that lead to the rise in feelings that lead some to consider and even attempt suicide?
This impacts my community because it is largely populated with teens whose behavior, beliefs, and states of mind may be reflected in the data shown in these graphs. It means that many of my students are not getting enough sleep, are persistently feeling hopeless or sad, and most troubling is the rise in considerations of suicide.
A potential headline:  “Is a Gram Better Than a Damn?”.

image_description:
1. **Chart type**: Multi-panel line chart (small multiples of time-series line charts).

2. **Layout techniques**:  
- Uses **small multiples/faceting**: each panel shows a different outcome/measure.  
- Within panels, multiple **lines** compare categories (e.g., male vs female, or different substances/behaviors).  
- No stacking.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Percentage / share of teens | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Measure / outcome (e.g., ever tried vaping, recently drank alcohol, ever had sex, watch television at least 3 hours a day, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; text labels inside panels |
| Substance/behavior within panel (e.g., cigarettes, vaping, alcohol, marijuana, cocaine; sex vs unprotected sex; television vs sleep) | Categorical/nominal | Separate line color/hue; direct text labels |
| Sex (male, female) | Categorical/nominal | Separate line color/hue; direct text labels |

**Visible panel measures/outcomes**:
- Ever tried vaping
- Ever tried cigarettes
- Recently drank alcohol
- Ever used marijuana
- Ever used cocaine
- Ever had sex
- Last sex was unprotected
- Watch television at least 3 hours a day
- Get at least 8 hours of sleep
- Use a smartphone, tablet, computer or game console at least 3 hours a day, not including school work
- Persistently felt sad or hopeless
- Seriously considered suicide
- Made a suicide plan
- Attempted suicide
- Injured in a suicide attempt and needed medical treatment
raw_comment:
I notice that females are more likely to feel sad or hopeless and have higher suicide consideration/rates/attempts than males. I also notice that although alcohol, vaping, and cigarette use have gone down, video game time has been gradually increasing. Suicide generally seems to be dropping since 1989 until about 2008-2009 when iphones became more widely used, and after the release in 2007.

How can we know that the youth surveyed by the CDC has provided accurate responses and not in fact skewed the data? How is the sample interviewed representative of the whole high school population. I also wonder if social media and digital devices have impacted drug, alcohol and vaping use.

As a student and teenager, I wonder how and if my peers will follow the current trend. I've seen adults and children alike increase their use of iphones.

My headline is: Among teenagers: How has mental health changed alongside drug and digital device use?

I notice that the rate of trying cigarettes has significantly decreased while marijuana use appears to be rising.

What do you wonder?
I wonder how accurate the data is based on who those surveyed were and how honest their answers were. In our generation, a lot of people keep what they've done and their feelings private due to the tendency of people to fear being shamed for their feelings. And so they keep thoughts of hopelessness and suicide private, and its often more common among males. As for drug use and sex because of the way our society is more males than females see it as a way of bragging. Thus, how accurate can this information be and how could fear have affected this data.
 
How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to me and my community because coming from a low-income community filled with a majority of Hispanics who have faced the struggles of unhealthy lifestyles and the acceptance of drug use affects how great the rates may be. As for mental health awareness, our community faces the struggles of many people of Hispanic backgrounds not knowing the damage of mental health issues and ignore or don't believe in its severity.

- Within panels, multiple **lines** compare categories (e.g., male vs female, or different substances/behaviors).  
- No stacking.

|---|---|---|

| Substance/behavior within panel (e.g., cigarettes, vaping, alcohol, marijuana, cocaine; sex vs unprotected sex; television vs sleep) | Categorical/nominal | Separate line color/hue; direct text labels |

Welcome to Wednesday's live moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  We will moderate until 2 pm ET.

Today’s graphs show the change in teen behaviors over a 30 year period (1989 – 2019) based on survey data by the CDC from thousands of high school students in private and public schools across the country.  Note that the time period precedes the Covid pandemic.

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?"  and “How will this affect you?”  Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas in these graphs. 

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the free link to the online article that included these graphs 
 
Note that you can get a link to your response (and replies made to it) to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs).
View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 
graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 
Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex).  

This is the last release of the school year. We will return in early September. You can receive the 2022-2023 “What’s Going On In This Graph?” schedule by subscribing to the New York Times Learning Network newsletter. In the meantime, keep noticing and wondering.

4. "Feeling sad? You're not the only one."
